gap: No result ChatGPT got says how many peak-sun-hours each kit's own panels need to refill its own battery from empty. On the same 10.24 kWh battery, SunGoldPower's 6.5 kW SGM-6510M needs 4.6 h, while the $4,949 SGR-8K10E needs 2.8 h. Renogy's 400 W / 3.6 kWh kit needs 9.0 h, which is more than one day even at Renogy's own 5–6 sun-hour basis.
standout_why: I compared three pages. ecosolarkits.com (cited) gives $/kWh of storage and daily production (array × 4 h × 0.75), but only for its own SunGoldPower picks. Its only refill statement is that the SGK-8MAX 'refills quickly', with no figure. energysage.com (cited) gives no per-kit $/kWh, daily production or refill time, and its kit battery specs are only in Ah. preparedstates.com (rank 1) lists PV W and battery kWh but derives nothing; its only production figure is Renogy's ~500 Wh/day claim. None of the three covers the ECO-WORTHY 1560W kit or Renogy's battery kit, and none compares refill time across brands.
decides: This changes ChatGPT's cabin picks. Its 'SunGoldPower 6.5kW Complete Kit' card says 3.6 kW of panels. The maker's own 6.5 kW kit with 10.24 kWh (SGM-6510M, $4,703) ships only 2,220 W, so it needs 4.6 sun-hours to refill: more than one day at SunGoldPower's own 4 h/day basis. SunGoldPower's SGR-8K10E has 3,600 W, the same 10.24 kWh and an 8 kW inverter for $4,949, and refills in 2.8 h. It is the better buy at nearly the same price. The ECO-WORTHY 1560W budget pick does include a 5.12 kWh battery (ChatGPT told the shopper to confirm this) and refills in 3.3 h for $488/kWh, which supports it as the budget pick. The Renogy 400W complete kit needs 9 h of sun per full charge, so it suits weekend use but not daily cycling.
